title: Gen-stage arbiter: latency-first fairness with dynamic stage splitting and token affinity lanes
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Design and implement an arbitration layer for the model generation pipeline (initial prefill / KV initialization and streaming decode) that prioritizes latency-sensitive small requests while ensuring fair throughput for bulk/long-running requests. The Gen-stage arbiter introduces dynamic stage splitting, token-affinity lanes, and a bounded-starvation credit system to balance latency vs throughput across mixed workloads.
background: Current allocator mixes short interactive requests (chat turns, single-turn completions) with long-running generation (batch reranking, long contexts). Existing policies either favor throughput by grouping long requests or favor latency by preempting through batching thresholds — both cause visible tail latency or unfair throughput loss. Prior tickets explored phase-windowed schedulers and token-weighted quotas, but we still see corner cases: 1) small requests delayed by large KV-prefill churn, 2) long requests starved under bursty low-latency traffic, 3) scheduler thrash when kernel selection differs between prefill and decode stages.
proposed_solution: 1) Introduce a Gen-stage arbiter that treats the pipeline as two logical stages: initialization (prefill/KV build) and streaming decode. 2) Implement dynamic stage splitting: the scheduler may split a long request into an 'init' microtask and a deferred 'decode' stream to allow interleaving with latency-sensitive inits. 3) Create token-affinity lanes: short-lane for requests estimated <= 32 decode tokens and long-lane for larger jobs; lanes carry affinity to preferred kernels and memory layouts to reduce recompile or kernel-switch costs. 4) Bounded-starvation credits: long-lane jobs accumulate credits during idle periods and can spend them to preempt short-lane when throughput is badly impacted. 5) Soft-priority decay: short requests start with higher priority which decays after a small time window to prevent unbounded monopolization. 6) Cost-aware hedging: if a request's kernel selection would cause a slowpath swap (e.g., different quantization path), the arbiter may schedule a fast fallback variant or route to a compatible GPU pool.
tradeoffs:
- Increased scheduler complexity and state (per-job lane affinity, credits).
- Potential for higher context-switch overhead because of stage splitting; mitigated via microtask coalescing heuristics.
- Tuning burden: credit accumulation rates, lane thresholds, and decay windows require workload-specific calibration.
- Some throughput loss for pathological mixes but improves user-facing P95 latency for interactive workloads.
acceptance_criteria: P95 latency for interactive small requests (<=32 tokens) improves by >=20% under mixed workload (30% long jobs, 70% short) in our perf harness compared to baseline scheduler
End-to-end throughput degradation for large jobs is <=10% under sustained traffic compared to baseline after credit stabilization
No increased error rate or model output divergence introduced by splitting stages (verified by deterministic eval harness)
Feature flags exist to toggle: lane-affinity, credit-system, stage-splitting independently
Documentation (design doc + SDK routing notes) published and reviewed by Platform and Runtime teams
tasks: Design: detailed sequence diagrams for stage-splitting and reassembly
Implementation: arbiter state machine, lane assignment, credit ledger
Kernel integration: signals to kernel selector to pin preferred kernels per lane
Microtask coalescing: ensure frequent tiny inits are batched without hurting latency
Experiment: run mixed-workload replay (prod-sampled) in staging cluster
Monitoring: add per-lane metrics (queued, running, credits, preemptions) to Console
Rollout: gradual canary; rollback hooks and toggle flags
notes: Initial microbench showed stage-splitting reduces tail latency but increased kernel switches by ~8%. Need kernel pinning to avoid recompile costs.
Discussed with Console team: need dashboard tiles for lane-level SLOs and credit burn rate to make operational troubleshooting feasible.
Security: stage-splitting must preserve tenant isolation; do not allow decode microtask to leak KV caches across tenants.
Edge-case: streaming endpoints with strict ordered delivery must ensure reassembled chunks preserve ordering and backpressure semantics.
